summary: For ages 9–11, this topic bridges two threads: (1) famous eruptions and how far their effects reach (Eyjafjallajökull 2010 ash grounding flights across Europe, a regional effect; Mount St Helens 1980; large explosive eruptions that send lots of sulphur gas high into the stratosphere, where it forms tiny droplets that reflect sunlight and cool global temperatures for months to a few years, while most ash falls out within days to weeks) and (2) Pangaea — continents were once joined and drifted apart, supported by converging evidence (coastline fit, matching fossils/rock bands, later seafloor data) and explained by plate movement. The load-bearing move is EVIDENCE→INFERENCE: coastline fit plus matching fossils support 'they were once joined and drifted apart'. Keep local devastation distinct from global atmospheric effects, and treat drift as slow (a few cm/year over hundreds of millions of years).
misconceptions: Continents are fixed and have always been where they are now (they ride plates and have drifted from a joined supercontinent).
Pangaea is just a guess (it is supported by converging evidence: coastline fit, matching fossils/rocks, seafloor data, and the plate mechanism).
Volcanoes only cause local damage (large explosive eruptions can affect global weather/climate via high-altitude ash and gas).
Eruptions warm the planet (major eruptions typically COOL global temperatures for a while by blocking sunlight).
Continental drift is fast / happened all at once (it is the same few-cm/year plate motion, adding up over hundreds of millions of years).

activities.title: Reassemble Pangaea, then check the evidence
steps: Cut out present-day continents (paper map) and move them around until the coastlines roughly fit together — notice South America nestling into Africa and how the pieces can be grouped into one approximate supercontinent (present-day coastlines and flat maps will leave gaps and overlaps).
Once assembled, overlay or draw on the areas of matching fossils (e.g. Mesosaurus, Glossopteris) and matching rock types so you can see them line up across the joins you just made.
State the inference in your own words: what do the puzzle-fit AND the matching fossils/rock together let you conclude, and why is each piece of evidence needed?
Estimate how long the break-up took if plates move only a few cm per year — relate that to 'hundreds of millions of years'.
Optionally, use a rotating globe (physical or digital) to rewind and watch the continents merge into Pangaea as a companion view of the same reassembly.
activities.insight: The conclusion 'continents were once joined and have drifted apart' is a reasoned inference from converging evidence (coastline fit + matching fossils/rock + slow plate motion), not a just-so story or a single guess.

activities.title: How a single volcano reaches the whole planet
steps: Pick a real eruption and trace how its ash cloud spread — e.g. map Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 ash creeping across Europe and grounding thousands of flights.

For a large explosive eruption, describe the chain: sulphur gas blasted high into the stratosphere forms a haze of tiny droplets that reflects sunlight, so less warmth reaches the surface and global temperatures can dip for months to a few years (most ash falls out within days to weeks).
Explain in writing or speech why the effect is COOLING, not warming, even though lava is hot — distinguish the tiny local heat from the global veil of sulphur droplets that reflects sunlight.
Contrast local devastation near the volcano (lava, blast, ashfall) with the GLOBAL effect carried through the atmosphere.
activities.insight: Large explosive eruptions that put lots of sulphur gas into the stratosphere can affect global weather/climate: the gas forms tiny droplets that reflect sunlight, temporarily cooling the planet — an atmospheric mechanism distinct from local lava damage, while ash mostly affects the region it drifts over.

activities.title: Study the before/after of a reshaped mountain
steps: Compare before-and-after images of Mount St Helens (1980) and describe how the lateral blast reshaped the mountain.
Describe at least one key effect of this famous eruption, separating the immediate local destruction from any wider atmospheric effects.

Connect eruption STYLE to reach: explain why an explosive eruption throws ash and gas higher, and why material that reaches higher can travel farther (and, if it includes lots of sulphur gas, can cool the climate more widely).
activities.insight: Eruption style governs both local reshaping and how far-reaching the effects are; explosive eruptions can loft material high enough to affect regions far from the volcano.

activities.title: Interview the scientist (optional spoken extension)
steps: Role-play or hold a discussion where one person takes the role of Alfred Wegener defending continental drift and must cite evidence (coastline fit, matching fossils/rock) when challenged.
Alternatively, interview a 'pilot grounded by Eyjafjallajökull ash' or a 'scientist at St Helens' to surface the human impact and the global reach of a single eruption.
Listeners ask follow-up questions that push for the mechanism, e.g. 'How do you KNOW they were joined?' or 'Why would ash so far away affect my flight?'
activities.insight: Scientific claims should be defended with evidence rather than asserted; voicing and challenging the reasoning out loud is intended to reinforce understanding of both the drift evidence and the global reach of eruptions.

checkQuestion: A huge volcano erupts and sends a giant cloud of ash and gas high into the sky. A friend says, 'All that hot lava and ash must make the whole planet warmer for a while.' Is that right? What effect can a big eruption have on temperatures around the world, and why?
checkAnswer: The friend is wrong — a big eruption usually COOLS the planet for a while. The ash and gases (like sulphur) rise high into the atmosphere and block or scatter some sunlight, so less warmth reaches the surface and global temperatures drop for months or years, even far from the volcano.
